body:
OBJECTIVES
- Students understand addition and subtraction of fractions as joining and separating parts of the same whole, decompose a fraction into a sum of fractions with the same denominator in more than one way, add and subtract mixed numbers with like denominators, and solve word problems (4.NF.B.3).
- Students understand a fraction a/b as a multiple of 1/b and multiply a fraction by a whole number, including in word problems (4.NF.B.4).

MATERIALS
- Fraction strips and fraction circles
- Number lines from 0 to 3 marked in fourths, sixths and eighths
- Paper plates or paper "pizzas" cut into eighths
- Measuring cups (1/4, 1/3, 1/2) for the recipe problems

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read Adding Pieces of the Same Size. Act out 2/8 + 3/8 with paper pizza slices. Lesson: Breaking Fractions Apart.
Day 2: Assignment: Pizza Party Fractions. Students model each problem with slices or a number line before writing an equation.
Day 3: Mixed numbers mini-lesson: show 1 3/4 with strips, then add another 2 2/4; regroup 5/4 as 1 1/4. Start Mixed Numbers on the Trail.
Day 4: Finish Mixed Numbers on the Trail. Repeated addition with measuring cups: fill a 2/3 cup four times and count the total. Connect to 4 × 2/3.
Day 5: Assessment: Adding and Subtracting Fractions Check.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: start every problem with a model (strips, circles or a number line) and keep denominators to fourths and eighths at first.
- Support: for subtraction with regrouping, have students rename the whole as a fraction first (3 1/8 = 2 9/8) with strips.
- Stretch: ask students to write their own two-step story problem with mixed numbers and trade with a partner.
- Multilingual learners: pre-teach mixed number, numerator, denominator and "in all" versus "left." Act out each word problem with objects so the language and the operation connect.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
We are adding and subtracting fractions this unit. When the pieces are the same size, we add the numerators and keep the denominator: 2/8 + 3/8 = 5/8. Cooking is perfect practice. If you bake together, ask your child: we need 3/4 cup of flour for one batch; how much for two batches? A pizza or a sandwich cut into equal pieces works well too.
title: Teacher guide: Adding Fractions
